title: Bēowulf
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 14–18, lines 371–455 (fitt VI). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t: Hrōðgār maþelode, helm Scyldinga:
sentences.l: Hrothgar spoke in speech-words, helm of the Scyldings:
sentences.i: Hrothgar spoke in formal words, protector of the Scyldings:
sentences.n: ‘maþelode’ is the past of ‘maþelian’, the verb that introduces a formal speech (as in Fitts III–V). ‘helm Scyldinga’ is in apposition to Hrōðgār: ‘helm’ is a helmet, a covering for the head, and so a protector, and ‘Scyldinga’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the Scyldings’, the Danes who descend from Scyld. The colon opens his answer to Wulfgār's report at the end of Fitt V.

sentences.t: ‘Ic hine cūðe cnihtwesende;
sentences.l: ‘I knew him, boy-being;
sentences.i: ‘I knew him when he was a boy;
sentences.n: ‘cūðe’ is the past of ‘cunnan’, ‘to know (a person)’, and ‘hine’ is its accusative object; the man meant is Beowulf, whom Wulfgār has just named to him (363), though Hrōðgār does not use the name here. ‘cnihtwesende’ is a present participle of a compound verb, ‘to be a boy’, and agrees with ‘hine’, so it tells when the knowing took place. The poem does not say here where or how Hrōðgār met him.

sentences.l: was his old-father called Ecgþēo, to whom Hrēþel of the Geats gave to home his only daughter;
sentences.i: His father was called Ecgþēo, and to him Hrēþel of the Geats gave his only daughter to take home as his wife;
sentences.n: ‘ealdfæder’ in other Old English texts means ‘grandfather, forefather’, but this man is Beowulf's father (Beowulf says ‘Wæs mīn fæder … Ecgþēow hāten’, ‘my father was called Ecgþēow’, at 262), so ‘old-father’ here must mean ‘father’; the ‘eald-’ may look back on a dead man, which is a guess. The apparatus shows that other editors print two words, ‘eald fæder’, ‘old father’. ‘Ecgþēo’ is the name Ecgþēow with the final -w missing in this spelling. ‘ðǣm’ is a dative, ‘to whom’, with ‘forgeaf’ (‘gave’) and ‘āngan dohtor’ (‘only daughter’, accusative, ‘āngan’ being a weak form of ‘ānga’). ‘tō hām forgeaf’ is the idiom for giving a woman in marriage. Hrēþel is the Geat king, Higelāc's father; so Beowulf's mother is Higelāc's sister, which is why Beowulf calls himself Higelāc's ‘mǣg’ below.

sentences.t:
is his eafora nū
heard hēr cumen, sōhte holdne wine.
sentences.l: his offspring is now, hard, come here; he sought a loyal friend.
sentences.i: His son, a hardy man, has now come here; he has sought out a loyal friend.
sentences.n: ‘is … cumen’ is a perfect made with ‘is’, not ‘hæfð’, as is usual for verbs of motion: ‘has come’. ‘eafora’ is ‘offspring, son’; Klaeber prints the final -a in italic because the manuscript has ‘eaforan’, which Kemble and Grundtvig corrected. ‘heard’ (‘hard’) is a predicate adjective for the son, in the sense ‘stout, bold’. The second clause has no subject stated: ‘sōhte holdne wine’, ‘(he) sought a loyal friend’, with ‘wine’ the accusative object; the friend is Hrōðgār himself, and the comma only marks a pause.

sentences.t:
Ðonne sægdon þæt sǣlīþende,
þā ðe gifsceattas Gēata fyredon
þyder tō þance, þæt hē þrītiges
manna mægencræft on his mundgripe
heaþorōf hæbbe.
sentences.l: Then said the sea-farers, those who carried the Geats' gift-treasures thither as a thanks, that he, battle-bold, has the might-strength of thirty of men in his hand-grip.
sentences.i: Moreover, the seafarers who carried the Geats' gift-treasures there as a token of thanks said that he, bold in battle, has in his hand-grip the strength of thirty men.
sentences.n: ‘Ðonne’ is a sentence-opening particle meaning ‘then’ or ‘moreover’; the reading is uncertain. ‘sǣlīþende’ is a nominative plural present participle used as a noun (‘sea-travelers’), and ‘þā ðe … fyredon’ is a relative clause, ‘those who carried’. ‘gifsceattas’ are ‘gift-treasures’ (‘sceatt’ is a coin or treasure); ‘tō þance’ is ‘as a thanks’, but the poem does not say here what the thanks were for. In the reported speech ‘hæbbe’ is a subjunctive, and ‘heaþorōf’ (‘battle-bold’) is an adjective in apposition to ‘hē’. ‘þrītiges manna’ is ‘of thirty of men’, a genitive of number; the apparatus gives the manuscript's figures as ‘.xxxtiges’, so the spelling out is Klaeber's.

sentences.t:
Hine hālig God
for ārstafum ūs onsende,
tō West-Denum, þæs ic wēn hæbbe,
wið Grendles gryre.
sentences.l: Him holy God, for favors, sent to us, to the West-Danes, as I have hope of that, against Grendel's terror.
sentences.i: Holy God, out of kindness, has sent him to us, to the West-Danes, as I hope, against the terror of Grendel.
sentences.n: ‘Hine’ is the accusative object, placed first for emphasis, and ‘ūs’ is a dative, ‘to us’. ‘for ārstafum’ is a dative plural, ‘for favors’ as with ‘mid ārstafum’ at 316 (Fitt IV): ‘ār’ is favor or mercy, ‘stæf’ a staff or support, so ‘acts of kindness’; the exact force of ‘-stafum’ is a guess. ‘þæs ic wēn hæbbe’ is ‘of which I have expectation’, with ‘þæs’ a genitive depending on ‘wēn’; it softens the claim to a hope. The Danes are named by direction, ‘West-Denum’, as ‘Ēast-Dena’ is below. ‘wið Grendles gryre’ takes the accusative, ‘against Grendel's terror’, the dread he spreads.

sentences.t:
Ic þǣm gōdan sceal
for his mōdþræce mādmas bēodan.
sentences.l: I to the good one shall, for his mind-force, offer treasures.
sentences.i: I shall offer treasures to the good man for his daring.
sentences.n: ‘sceal’ with an infinitive can mean ‘shall’ or ‘must’; here it is both a promise and a duty. ‘þǣm gōdan’ is a dative, ‘to the good one’, a weak adjective used as a noun for Beowulf. ‘bēodan’ takes the dative of the person and the accusative of the gift, ‘mādmas’. ‘mōdþræce’ is a rare compound of ‘mōd’, ‘mind, spirit’, and ‘þræc’, ‘force, boldness’; ‘daring’ is a guess at its sense. The king pays for courage before it is shown: a lord's treasure is the return for his man's boldness, and here it is offered in advance.

sentences.t:
Bēo ðū on ofeste, hāt in gân
sēon sibbegedriht samod ætgædere;
sentences.l: Be you in haste, bid the kin-band go in to see, together at once;
sentences.i: Be quick, and bid this loyal company go in and see me, all together;
sentences.n: ‘Bēo’ is the imperative of ‘bēon’, ‘be’, with ‘ðū’ ‘you’ after it; ‘on ofeste’ is ‘in haste’; ‘hāt’ is the imperative of ‘hātan’, ‘bid’. The order is addressed to Wulfgār, who stands by. In ‘hāt in gân sēon sibbegedriht’ the accusative ‘sibbegedriht’ is the object of ‘hāt’ and also the subject of ‘gân sēon’, ‘go in (and) see’, moved to the end of the sentence; the person they are to see, Hrōðgār, is understood. ‘sibbegedriht’ is a compound of ‘sibb’, ‘kinship, peace’, and ‘gedriht’, ‘company’; ‘kin-band’ is a guess in the word-for-word line, since these men are not Hrōðgār's kin but a band bound by loyalty to one lord; the idiomatic line therefore says ‘loyal company’. The apparatus lists several editors who change ‘sēon’; Klaeber leaves it.

sentences.t:
gesaga him ēac wordum, þæt hīe sint wilcuman
Deniga lēodum.’
sentences.l: tell them also in words that they are welcome-comers to the Danes' people.’
sentences.i: and tell them also, in so many words, that they are welcome to the Danish people.’
sentences.n: ‘gesaga’ is the imperative of ‘gesecgan’, ‘tell’, with ‘him’ a dative, ‘to them’. ‘wordum’ is a dative of means: ‘in words’, that is, plainly said and not left to be understood. ‘wilcuman’ is a plural noun built from ‘wil-’, ‘pleasure’, and ‘cuma’, ‘comer’: the source of our ‘welcome’. ‘Deniga lēodum’ is a dative, ‘to the people of the Danes’. The closing quotation mark ends Hrōðgār's speech.

sentences.t:
[Þā wið duru healle
Wulfgār ēode,] word inne ābēad:
sentences.l: [Then Wulfgar went to the door of the hall,] announced a word within:
sentences.i: [Then Wulfgar went to the door of the hall,] and from within he called out his message:
sentences.n: The brackets mean Klaeber added these words by emendation: the manuscript goes straight from Hrōðgār's speech to ‘word inne ābēad’, without saying who speaks, and the apparatus says Grein supplied the half-lines and that Ettmüller inserted four. Wulfgār's name and journey are therefore conjecture, but he is the only messenger in the scene, so little is risked. ‘wið duru healle’ is ‘to the door of the hall’ (‘wið’ with the accusative, ‘duru’ a feminine noun, ‘healle’ a genitive). ‘ābēad’ is the past of ‘ābēodan’, ‘announce’, with ‘word’ as object. ‘inne’ is ‘within’; it is not clear whether he speaks from the inner side of the door to the Geats waiting outside, which is the likelier picture.

sentences.t:
‘Ēow hēt secgan sigedrihten mīn,
aldor Ēast-Dena, þæt hē ēower æþelu can,
ond gē him syndon ofer sǣwylmas
heardhicgende hider wilcuman.
sentences.l: ‘To you my victory-lord bade say, the chief of the East-Danes, that he knows your noble-descent, and you are to him over the sea-surges, hard-minded, welcome-comers here.
sentences.i: ‘My victorious lord, the chief of the East-Danes, bids me tell you that he knows your noble lineage, and that you, stout of heart, are welcome to him here, come over the surge of the sea.
sentences.n: ‘hēt secgan’ is ‘bade say’ (‘hēt’ is the past of ‘hātan’, followed by an infinitive); the person ordered, Wulfgār himself, is not named, and ‘Ēow’ is the dative, ‘to you’. Two ‘þæt’-clauses follow, joined by ‘ond’: ‘hē … can’ (‘he knows’, ‘can’ being the present of ‘cunnan’) with ‘ēower æþelu’ as object, and ‘gē … syndon … wilcuman’, ‘you are welcome-comers’, with ‘him’ a dative of the host. ‘sigedrihten’ is ‘victory-lord’, a lord who gives or wins victory; ‘aldor’ is ‘chief, lord’; ‘ofer sǣwylmas’ is ‘over the surges of the sea’, with ‘wylm’ the well-up or surge of water. ‘heardhicgende’ is ‘hard-thinking’, so resolute, stout-hearted. A herald repeats the king's welcome in the king's own formal terms.

sentences.t:
Nū gē mōton gangan in ēowrum gūðsearwum,
under heregrīman Hrōðgār gesēon;
sentences.l: Now you may go in your war-gear, under army-masks, to see Hrothgar;
sentences.i: Now you may go forward in your battle-dress and under your helmets to see Hrothgar;
sentences.n: ‘mōton’ is the present plural of ‘mōtan’, ‘be allowed to’: permission, not command. ‘gangan’ is the infinitive that ‘mōton’ governs, and ‘gesēon’ (‘to see’) adds the purpose. ‘gūðsearwum’ is a dative plural of ‘gūðsearu’, ‘war-gear’; Klaeber prints ‘sear’ in italic because the manuscript has ‘geata’ with ‘wum’ on the next line, which editors read ‘-getāwum’ or ‘-geatwum’ (both ‘equipment’); ‘-searwum’ is Holthausen's, and all the readings give nearly the same sense. ‘heregrīman’ is a dative plural, ‘army-masks’, the face-covering helmets; compare the ‘mask-helmets’ (‘grīmhelmas’) of Fitt V, 334. Hrōðgār lets the visitors enter armed, but the next unit takes their shields and spears.

sentences.t:
lǣtað hildebord hēr onbīdan,
wudu wælsceaftas worda geþinges.’
sentences.l: let battle-boards wait here, the wood, the slaughter-shafts, for the words' settlement.’
sentences.i: leave your shields here, and your deadly spears, to wait for the result of the talking.’
sentences.n: ‘lǣtað’ is the plural imperative of ‘lǣtan’, ‘let’, followed by the infinitive ‘onbīdan’, ‘wait’. The manuscript reads ‘on bidman’ with an incomplete erasure of the m; Thorkelin has ‘on bidian’, and Klaeber prints ‘onbīdan’ (the apparatus). ‘hildebord’ is ‘battle-board’, a shield, and ‘wudu’ and ‘wælsceaftas’ (‘slaughter-shafts’) are spears: ‘wudu’, ‘wood’, can stand for the shaft. ‘onbīdan’ takes a genitive, so ‘worda geþinges’ is ‘for the words' settlement’ (literally ‘of words, of the agreement’): ‘geþing’ is an agreement, a conference or the settlement reached; which of these is meant is not certain. The shields and spears wait for the talk to be finished; the closing mark ends Wulfgār's speech.

sentences.t:
Ārās þā se rīca, ymb hine rinc manig,
þrȳðlīc þegna hēap;
sentences.l: Arose then the mighty one, about him many a warrior, a strong heap of thanes;
sentences.i: Then the mighty one rose, and around him many warriors, a strong band of thanes;
sentences.n: ‘Ārās’ is the past of ‘ārīsan’, ‘arise’. ‘se rīca’ is ‘the mighty one’, a weak adjective used as a noun, and the man meant is Beowulf, whom the narrator does not name until 405. ‘ymb hine rinc manig’ is ‘around him many a warrior’, and ‘þrȳðlīc þegna hēap’ is a second phrase, ‘a strong (or splendid) band of thanes’, that restates it. ‘þrȳðlīc’ comes from ‘þrȳð’, ‘strength, glory’. ‘hēap’ is a ‘heap’, as in English, but in the poem it is a body of men.

sentences.t:
sume þǣr bidon,
heaðorēaf hēoldon, swā him se hearda bebēad.
sentences.l: some remained there, kept the battle-gear, as the hard one bade them.
sentences.i: Some stayed behind there, to guard the war-gear, as their stern leader had told them.
sentences.n: ‘sume’ is a nominative plural, ‘some (of them)’, and ‘bidon’ is the past plural of ‘bīdan’, ‘remain’. ‘heaðorēaf hēoldon’ is a second clause with the same subject and no ‘and’ (‘kept the battle-gear’): ‘rēaf’ is clothing or plunder, and ‘heaðorēaf’ is the war-dress and weapons. ‘swā him se hearda bebēad’ is ‘as the hard one commanded them’, with ‘bebēad’ the past of ‘bebēodan’ and ‘him’ a dative. ‘se hearda’ is Beowulf again, ‘the hard (brave) one’. The poem tells us only now that he left some of his band outside.

sentences.t:
Snyredon ætsomne — secg wīsode —
under Heorotes hrōf;
sentences.l: They hastened together — the man showed the way — under Heorot's roof;
sentences.i: They hurried in together, the warrior guiding them, under the roof of Heorot;
sentences.n: ‘Snyredon’ is the past plural of ‘snyrian’, ‘to hasten’, a rare verb. The dashes are Klaeber's: ‘secg wīsode’, ‘the man showed the way’, is an aside, with the verb used of the path at 320 (‘stīg wīsode’, Fitt V). The Thorkelin copies have ‘þā’ before ‘secg’, which Sievers and later editors delete and Klaeber omits (apparatus). The guide is not named; he is probably Wulfgār, who has just delivered the message, but that is an inference. ‘under Heorotes hrōf’ is ‘under Heorot's roof’, the hall introduced in the prologue.

sentences.t:
[heaþorinc ēode,]
heard under helme, þæt hē on heo[r]ðe gestōd.
sentences.l: [the battle-man went,] hard under helmet, until he stood on the hearth.
sentences.i: [the warrior walked in,] stern under his helmet, until he stood at the hearth.
sentences.n: The brackets mean the half-line is Klaeber's supply: the manuscript lacks it, and the apparatus shows Grein's ‘hygerōf ēode’ (‘the brave-minded went’) and Ettmüller's longer insertion beside Klaeber's ‘heaþorinc ēode’; the subject is clearly Beowulf. ‘heard under helme’ repeats the phrase used of him in Fitt V. ‘þæt hē … gestōd’ is a clause with the past ‘gestōd’, here ‘until he stood’. ‘heo[r]ðe’ has an [r] that editors added to the manuscript's ‘heoðe’ to make ‘heorðe’, a dative of ‘heorð’, ‘hearth’; Bugge proposed ‘hlēoðe’, ‘within hearing’, which makes a different sense, so the hearth is a probable reading, not a sure one.

sentences.t:
Bēowulf maðelode — on him byrne scān,
searonet seowed smiþes orþancum —:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words — on him the byrnie shone, the armor-net sewn by the smith's craft-thoughts —:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words — on him the mail-coat shone, that net of armor stitched by the smith's skill —:
sentences.n: ‘maðelode’ is the same verb as ‘maþelode’; ð and þ are two letters for one sound in Klaeber's print. The dashes set off a picture while he speaks. ‘byrne’ is the subject of ‘scān’, ‘shone’, and ‘searonet’ (‘armor-net’) restates it as a kenning for mail, which is a net of linked rings. ‘seowed’ is the participle of ‘siwian’, ‘sew’, so the rings are sewn or stitched together; ‘orþancum’ is a dative plural, ‘by the ingenious thoughts’, of ‘orþanc’, ‘cleverness’, and ‘smiþes’ is the smith's genitive. The colon after the second dash opens Beowulf's long speech, which runs to the end of the part.

sentences.t: ‘Wæs þū, Hrōðgār, hāl!
sentences.l: ‘Be you, Hrothgar, hale!
sentences.i: ‘Health to you, Hrothgar!
sentences.n: ‘Wæs’ looks like the past ‘was’, but here it is the imperative, ‘be’, as the apparatus notes; Kemble and others print ‘wes’, as in ‘wes þū ūs lārena gōd’ in Fitt IV, and Klaeber keeps the manuscript's ‘wæs’. ‘hāl’ is ‘whole, healthy’, and ‘wæs hāl’ is the greeting that has come down to us as ‘wassail’ and ‘hail’. The vocative ‘Hrōðgār’ is set inside it.

sentences.t:
Ic eom Higelāces
mǣg ond magoðegn;
sentences.l: I am Higelac's kinsman and young-thane;
sentences.i: I am Higelac's kinsman and thane;
sentences.n: ‘mǣg’ is ‘kinsman’; Beowulf is Higelāc's sister's son, though the line does not say so. ‘magoðegn’ is a compound of ‘magu’, ‘young man, son’, and ‘ðegn’, ‘thane’ (a retainer who serves a lord); the first part may also point to blood-kinship, so ‘young-thane’ is a choice among possibilities. The two titles together put his two claims on Hrōðgār's ear: he is both kin of his lord and his lord's sworn man.

sentences.t:
hæbbe ic mǣrða fela
ongunnen on geogoþe.
sentences.l: I have of glories many begun in youth.
sentences.i: I have undertaken many glorious deeds in my youth.
sentences.n: ‘hæbbe ic … ongunnen’ is a perfect, ‘I have begun, undertaken’, with the verb and the participle apart. ‘mǣrða’ is a genitive plural of ‘mǣrþu’, ‘glorious deeds’, depending on ‘fela’, ‘many’. ‘on geogoþe’ is ‘in youth’, a dative. The line is the usual way for a warrior to name his credentials before speaking of the task.

sentences.t:
Mē wearð Grendles þing
on mīnre ēþeltyrf undyrne cūð;
sentences.l: To me became Grendel's affair, in my native turf, not hidden, known;
sentences.i: Grendel's doings became plainly known to me in my own native land;
sentences.n: ‘Mē’ is a dative, ‘to me’, with ‘wearð … cūð’, ‘became known’ (‘wearð’ is the past of ‘weorðan’, ‘become’). ‘þing’ is ‘thing, affair, matter’; it is the same word as the ‘ðing’ of the assembly at 426, so ‘Grendles þing’ is ‘Grendel's business’. ‘ēþeltyrf’ is ‘native turf’, the soil of the fatherland, and ‘on mīnre ēþeltyrf’ is ‘in my homeland’. ‘undyrne’ is ‘not hidden’, so ‘openly’. The report has crossed the sea, which prepares the reasons given next.

sentences.t:
secgað sǣlīðend, þæt þæs sele stande,
reced sēlesta rinca gehwylcum
īdel ond unnyt, siððan ǣfenlēoht
under heofenes haðor beholen weorþeð.
sentences.l: Seafarers say that this hall stands, the best hall, idle and useless to each of men, after evening-light under heaven's brightness becomes hidden.
sentences.i: Seafarers say that this hall, the best of buildings, stands idle and useless to every man, once the evening light is hidden under the clear heaven.
sentences.n: ‘secgað’ is a present plural, and the ‘þæt’-clause has a subjunctive, ‘stande’, because it reports speech. ‘þæs sele’ is ‘this hall’: the manuscript has ‘þæs’ for ‘þes’ (the apparatus shows that Kemble and others print ‘þes’), and Klaeber keeps the manuscript. ‘rinca gehwylcum’ is a dative, ‘to each of men’, meaning ‘for every man’; ‘īdel ond unnyt’ say what the hall is. ‘ǣfenlēoht’ is the subject of ‘weorþeð’ (‘becomes’), with ‘beholen’, ‘hidden’, as a participle. ‘haðor’ is a rare word, ‘brightness, clearness’ of the sky, and ‘heaven's brightness’ is a guess; Klaeber prints the ð in italic because the manuscript has ‘hador’. After dark the hall is left empty, because Grendel comes at night.

sentences.t:
Þā mē þæt gelǣrdon lēode mīne,
þā sēlestan, snotere ceorlas,
þēoden Hrōðgār, þæt ic þē sōhte,
sentences.l: Then my people taught me that, the best, wise churls, prince Hrothgar, that I should seek you,
sentences.i: Then my people, the best of them, wise men and free, advised me, lord Hrothgar, to come and seek you out,
sentences.n: ‘Þā’ is an adverb, ‘then’, and ‘mē’ is a dative. The first ‘þæt’ is a pronoun anticipating the second: ‘taught me that, namely that I should seek you’; ‘gelǣrdon’ is the past plural of ‘gelǣran’, ‘teach, advise’. ‘lēode’ is nominative plural; ‘sēlestan’ and ‘snotere ceorlas’ describe the same people, ‘ceorl’ being a free man of the lower rank. ‘þēoden Hrōðgār’ is a vocative, ‘lord Hrothgar’, set inside the sentence. ‘sōhte’ is a past subjunctive after a verb of advice (the first-person form is the same in the indicative, so the sense decides).

sentences.t: forþan hīe mægenes cræft mīn[n]e cūþon;
sentences.l: because they knew my power of strength;
sentences.i: since they knew my great strength;
sentences.n: ‘forþan’ is ‘because’, and ‘hīe’ is the same people, ‘they’. ‘mægenes cræft’ is ‘power of strength’: ‘cræft’ (‘power, skill’) is the accusative object, ‘mægenes’ its genitive, and ‘mīn[n]e’, a masculine accusative, agrees with ‘cræft’, so ‘my power’. The apparatus says the manuscript has ‘mine’ for ‘minne’, and Klaeber's brackets mark the added n in ‘mīn[n]e’.

sentences.t:
selfe ofersāwon, ðā ic of searwum cwōm,
fāh from fēondum, þǣr ic fīfe geband,
sentences.l: themselves saw it, when I from the war-gear came, stained from foes, where I bound five,
sentences.i: they saw it themselves, when I came out of my armor, stained with my foes' blood, there where I bound five,
sentences.n: ‘selfe ofersāwon’ is ‘themselves saw’; ‘ofersāwon’ is the past plural of ‘ofersēon’, ‘look upon’, with no object stated. ‘ðā ic of searwum cwōm’ is ‘when I came out of the war-gear’; ‘searu’ can mean armor or a device, a trap, and the apparatus lists Grein's ‘on’ for ‘of’; which sense is meant here is a guess, and the translation ‘out of the war-gear’ is the plainer one. ‘fāh from fēondum’ is ‘stained from foes’, with ‘fāh’ in the sense ‘stained’ (the blood is understood) (compare ‘drēore fāhne’ at 447), a guess, since ‘fāh’ can also mean ‘hostile’. ‘fīfe geband’ is ‘bound five’, but the apparatus lists a string of editors who read ‘fīfel’ or ‘fīfelgeban’ (‘monster’, ‘sea’) instead, so the line is disputed. Taken as Klaeber prints it, ‘fīfe’ is a bare number: five of what is not said (the giants of the next line are the natural guess).

sentences.t:
ȳðde eotena cyn, ond on ȳðum slōg
niceras nihtes, nearoþearfe drēah,
wræc Wedera nīð — wēan āhsodon —,
forgrand gramum;
sentences.l: laid waste the kin of giants, and on the waves slew sea-monsters by night, endured narrow-distress, avenged the Weders' affliction — they asked for woes —, ground down the fierce ones;
sentences.i: I laid waste the race of giants, and on the waves I slew sea-monsters by night; I endured bitter straits and avenged the affliction of the Weders — they had asked for woe —, and crushed the fierce ones;
sentences.n: ‘ȳðde’, ‘slōg’, ‘drēah’, ‘wræc’ and ‘forgrand’ are first person past and share ‘ic’ from 420; ‘āhsodon’ is third plural. ‘ȳðde’ is from ‘ȳðan’, ‘to lay waste’ (a different word from ‘ȳð’, ‘wave’, in ‘on ȳðum’, ‘on the waves’). ‘niceras’ are ‘water-monsters’, ‘nihtes’ a genitive of time. ‘nearoþearfe drēah’ is ‘suffered narrow need’, ‘drēah’ being the past of ‘drēogan’. ‘wræc Wedera nīð’ is ‘avenged the Weders' affliction’, with ‘Wedera’ the Geats' other name. ‘wēan āhsodon’ (‘asked for woes’) has no stated subject; the beasts who brought trouble on themselves is the likelier sense, but it is a guess. ‘forgrand’ is the past of ‘forgrindan’; ‘gramum’ is a dative plural, ‘the fierce ones’.

sentences.t:
ond nū wið Grendel sceal,
wið þām āglǣcan āna gehēgan
ðing wið þyrse.
sentences.l: and now against Grendel I shall, against the awesome one, alone hold an assembly, a thing against the giant.
sentences.i: and now I must hold a meeting with Grendel, that fearsome one, alone, a reckoning with the giant.
sentences.n: ‘sceal’ has its infinitive in ‘gehēgan’, ‘carry through, hold’, and its object is ‘ðing’: ‘þing gehēgan’ is the phrase for holding a legal assembly to settle a case. Here it is a grim figure for the fight: Beowulf will settle things with Grendel as a court would, only with hands. ‘āglǣcan’ is a dative singular of ‘āglǣca’, ‘the awesome one’, the disputed word glossed in Fitt II (the same word is spelled ‘ǣglǣca’ at 433), and ‘āna’ is ‘alone’. ‘þyrs’ is ‘giant, ogre’, a second name for Grendel. ‘wið’ takes the accusative in ‘wið Grendel’ (the apparatus lists the dative ‘Grendle’) and the dative in ‘wið þām āglǣcan’ and ‘wið þyrse’, where ‘þyrse’ is a dative singular.

sentences.t:
Ic þē nū ðā,
brego Beorht-Dena, biddan wille,
eodor Scyldinga, ānre bēne,
sentences.l: I will ask you now then, ruler of the Bright-Danes, fence of the Scyldings, for one boon,
sentences.i: Now then, lord of the Bright-Danes, shield of the Scyldings, I wish to ask you for one favor,
sentences.n: ‘Ic þē … biddan wille’ is ‘I will ask you’, with ‘wille’ here an auxiliary, ‘will, wish’. ‘biddan’ takes the person asked in the accusative and the thing asked for in the genitive, ‘ānre bēne’, ‘one request’. ‘brego’ is ‘prince, ruler’, and ‘Beorht-Dena’ is ‘of the Bright-Danes’, a genitive plural with the Danes named by a flattering epithet. ‘eodor’ is a ‘fence’, an enclosure, and so a protector: ‘eodor Scyldinga’ is the kenning for the king as the fence that guards his people. The next unit says what the favor is.

sentences.t:
þæt ðū mē ne forwyrne, wīgendra hlēo,
frēowine folca, nū ic þus feorran cōm,
þæt ic mōte āna [ond] mīnra eorla gedryht,
þes hearda hēap, Heorot fǣlsian.
sentences.l: that you not refuse me, shelter of warriors, noble-friend of peoples, now that I have come thus from afar, that I may, alone, and my earls' company, this hard heap, cleanse Heorot.
sentences.i: that you will not refuse me, protector of warriors, noble friend of peoples, now that I have come thus from so far away: that I and the company of my earls, this hardy band, on our own may cleanse Heorot.
sentences.n: ‘þæt ðū mē ne forwyrne’ is a subjunctive, ‘that you not refuse me’, in a request; the thing refused is the second ‘þæt’-clause, ‘þæt ic mōte … fǣlsian’, ‘that I may cleanse’ (‘mōte’ is the present subjunctive of ‘mōtan’, ‘be permitted’). ‘hlēo’ is ‘shelter’, and ‘frēowine’ is ‘noble friend’ (the apparatus shows ‘frēawine’, ‘lord and friend’, in other editions). The manuscript has ‘ond’ before ‘þes’; Klaeber, following Kemble, moves it to the bracketed position after ‘āna’, which makes Beowulf and his company one subject. ‘þes hearda hēap’ restates the company. ‘fǣlsian’ is ‘cleanse, purify’, as of a stain.

sentences.t:
Hæbbe ic ēac geāhsod, þæt se ǣglǣca
for his wonhȳdum wǣpna ne recceð;
sentences.l: I have also learned by asking, that the awesome one, for his lack-of-heed, cares not for weapons;
sentences.i: I have also learned that the fearsome one, in his recklessness, cares nothing for weapons;
sentences.n: ‘Hæbbe ic … geāhsod’ is a perfect: ‘geāhsian’ is to learn by asking. ‘ǣglǣca’ is a spelling of the ‘āglǣca’ of 425, the disputed ‘awesome one’ of Fitt II. ‘recceð’ is the present of ‘reccan’, ‘to care for’, and takes the genitive ‘wǣpna’; ‘ne’ negates it. ‘wonhȳdum’ is a dative plural of an obscure word, apparently ‘won’, ‘lacking’, and ‘hȳd’, ‘care, heed’ (perhaps related to ‘hygd’, ‘thought’), so ‘lack of heed’ and then ‘recklessness’; that is a guess. ‘for’ gives the reason, ‘because of’. Because Grendel ignores weapons, Beowulf will not use them.

sentences.t:
ic þæt þonne forhicge, swā mē Higelāc sīe,
mīn mondrihten mōdes blīðe,
sentences.l: I that then scorn, so may Higelac be to me, my man-lord, blithe of mind,
sentences.i: I therefore scorn it — so may Higelac, my liege lord, be kindly in mind to me —
sentences.n: ‘þonne’ is ‘then’, ‘in that case’, which the idiomatic line renders ‘therefore’. ‘forhicge’ is the present of ‘forhycgan’, ‘scorn, disdain’; ‘þæt’ looks forward to the clause in 437, ‘that I bear sword or shield’. ‘swā mē Higelāc sīe’ is ‘so may Higelāc be to me’, a wish used like an oath: Beowulf wants his lord's favor as surely as he means what he says; ‘sīe’ is a present subjunctive, and the apparatus lists Sievers's ‘sī’. ‘mondrihten’ is ‘lord of men’, a title for a liege; ‘mōdes blīðe’ is ‘glad of mind’, a genitive of respect.

sentences.t:
þæt ic sweord bere oþðe sīdne scyld,
geolorand tō gūþe,
sentences.l: that I bear sword or broad shield, yellow-rim, to battle,
sentences.i: that I should carry sword or broad shield, the yellow shield, to the fight,
sentences.n: ‘þæt ic … bere’ is a present subjunctive clause that explains ‘þæt’ in 435: what he scorns. ‘oþðe’ is ‘or’. ‘sīdne scyld’ is ‘broad shield’, accusative, and ‘geolorand’ is ‘yellow rim’ (‘geolo’, ‘yellow’; ‘rand’, ‘rim’), a poetic word for a shield from its yellow rim (painted or of limewood is a guess). ‘tō gūþe’ is ‘to battle’. He will wrestle with his bare hands, for the reason in the previous unit.

sentences.l: but I with a grip shall seize against the foe and strive about life, hated one against hated one;
sentences.i: but with my grip I must grapple with the enemy and strive for life, foe against foe;
sentences.n: ‘mid grāpe’ is ‘with a grip’, a dative; ‘sceal’ governs the two infinitives, ‘fōn’ (‘seize, take hold’) and ‘sacan’ (‘strive, contend’). ‘fōn wið fēonde’ is ‘to grapple with the enemy’, and ‘ymb feorh’ is ‘about life’, the life at stake. ‘lāð wið lāþum’ is ‘hated one against hated one’: the dative ending of ‘lāþum’ can be singular or plural, and the singular gives ‘foe against foe’. The word-order throws the weight on ‘mid grāpe’, the hand against the weapon.

sentences.t:
ðǣr gelȳfan sceal
Dryhtnes dōme sē þe hine dēað nimeð.
sentences.l: there shall trust in the Lord's judgment he whom death takes.
sentences.i: There he whom death takes must trust in the Lord's judgment.
sentences.n: ‘ðǣr’ is ‘there’, in the fight just described. ‘gelȳfan’ takes the dative, ‘Dryhtnes dōme’, ‘in the Lord's judgment’. ‘sē þe hine dēað nimeð’ is ‘he whom death takes’, a relative clause, with ‘hine’ repeating the relative. ‘Dryhten’ is ‘Lord’, here God. The line states that whichever man dies, the outcome is God's decision: the Christian voice of the poet in Beowulf's mouth, as at 381.

sentences.t:
Wēn’ ic þæt hē wille, gif hē wealdan mōt,
in þǣm gūðsele Gēotena lēode
etan unforhte, swā hē oft dyde,
mægenhrēð manna.
sentences.l: I expect that he will, if he may rule, in the war-hall eat the Geats' people fearlessly, as he oft did, the might-glory of men.
sentences.i: I expect that he intends, if he is allowed to have his way, to devour the Geat folk fearlessly in that hall of battle, as he has often done, the strength and glory of men.
sentences.n: ‘Wēn’ ic’: the mark after ‘Wēn’ stands for a dropped e (‘wēne ic’, ‘I expect’) before ‘ic’; it is not a closing quotation mark, and the speech continues. ‘þæt hē wille … etan’ is ‘that he intends to eat’; ‘gif hē wealdan mōt’ is ‘if he is allowed to rule’ (‘mōt’, ‘may’). ‘gūðsele’ is ‘war-hall’, Heorot, named for the fighting. ‘Gēotena’ is the manuscript's form, a variant of ‘Gēata’; the apparatus lists many emendations, and Klaeber keeps it. ‘unforhte’ is most simply an adverb, ‘fearlessly’, with ‘etan’; it could also be the accusative plural ‘fearless’ with ‘lēode’, which would call the victims fearless; the adverb is the simpler choice. ‘mægenhrēð’ is a rare compound, apparently ‘strength-glory’, which restates ‘Gēotena lēode’; that sense is a guess, as the apparatus shows other editors split or change it. ‘swā hē oft dyde’ is ‘as he often did’.

sentences.t:
Nā þū mīnne þearft
hafalan hȳdan,
sentences.l: Not you need my head to hide,
sentences.i: You will have no need to hide my head,
sentences.n: ‘Nā … þearft’ is ‘not … need’: ‘þearft’ is the second person singular present of ‘þurfan’, ‘need’, with the infinitive ‘hȳdan’, ‘hide’. ‘hafalan’ is the accusative of ‘hafola’, ‘head’. To hide a head probably means to bury the body, so the line says Hrōðgār will have no burial to see to; the next lines say why.

sentences.t:
ac hē mē habban wile
d[r]ēore fāhne, gif mec dēað nimeð;
sentences.l: but he will have me, gore-stained, if death takes me;
sentences.i: but he will have me, stained with gore, if death takes me;
sentences.n: ‘ac’ is ‘but’: ‘hē’ is Grendel, and ‘habban wile’ is ‘will have, will hold’. ‘mē … fāhne’ is accusative: ‘fāhne’ is ‘stained’, as at 420, and ‘drēore’ is a dative, ‘with gore’. The manuscript has ‘deore’; Grundtvig and Kemble added the r, which Klaeber's bracket marks. ‘gif mec dēað nimeð’ is ‘if death takes me’, with ‘mec’ an older form of ‘mē’ (accusative) and a plain present indicative, as at 441.

sentences.l: he bears away the bloody slaughter, means to taste it, the lone-goer eats without grief, marks the moor-hollows;
sentences.i: He will bear off the bloody carcass and mean to taste it; the lone prowler will eat without sorrow and leave his mark on his haunts in the moor;
sentences.n: All the verbs are present in the sense ‘will’, with Grendel as subject. ‘wæl’ is ‘slaughter, the slain’, here the body, and ‘blōdig’ is ‘bloody’. ‘byrgean’ is ‘taste’ and ‘þenceð’ is ‘intends’. ‘āngenga’ is ‘lone-goer’, a nominative for Grendel; ‘unmurnlīce’ is ‘without mourning’. ‘mearcað mōrhopu’ is uncertain: ‘mearcian’ is ‘to mark’, and ‘hop’ is a retreat in the fen, so he marks the moor-hollows, perhaps with blood (a guess), though ‘marks out’ is also possible.

sentences.t:
nō ðū ymb mīnes ne þearft
līces feorme leng sorgian.
sentences.l: no, you need not about my body's feeding any longer sorrow.
sentences.i: Nor need you trouble yourself any longer about the feeding of my body.
sentences.n: ‘nō … ne þearft’ is a doubled negative that stresses the denial. ‘ymb … feorme’ is ‘about the feeding’; ‘mīnes … līces’ is a genitive pair, ‘of my body’, and the words ‘ymb mīnes’ and ‘līces feorme’ are split. ‘feorme’ is an accusative of ‘feorm’ (‘ymb’ takes the accusative), ‘provision, entertainment, food’; whether it means Grendel's meal or the cost of Beowulf's funeral is unclear, and the sense is much the same. ‘leng’ is ‘longer’ and ‘sorgian’ is ‘to be anxious’.

sentences.l: Send to Higelac, if battle takes me, of battle-garments the best, that guards my breast, of garments the choicest;
sentences.i: If battle takes me, send to Higelac the best of battle-dress, which guards my breast, the choicest of garments;
sentences.n: ‘Onsend’ is the imperative of ‘onsendan’; ‘Higelāce’ is the dative, ‘to Higelac’. ‘gif mec hild nime’ is a subjunctive, ‘if battle should take me’, ‘hild’ being ‘battle’. ‘beaduscrūda betst’ and ‘hrægla sēlest’ are two phrases for the same mail-coat, ‘best of battle-garments’ and ‘choicest of garments’, with genitive plurals; ‘þæt’ is the relative pronoun, ‘which’, and ‘wereð’ is the present of ‘werian’, ‘guard’. Beowulf means the byrnie that shone in 405: the one thing of value he asks to be sent home.

sentences.t:
þæt is Hrǣdlan lāf,
Wēlandes geweorc.
sentences.l: that is Hrædla's leaving, Weland's work.
sentences.i: It is Hrædla's heirloom, the work of Weland.
sentences.n: ‘lāf’ is ‘what is left’, a legacy or heirloom. ‘Hrǣdlan’ is a genitive of ‘Hrǣdla’; the apparatus shows editors who print ‘Hrēðlan’, and the name is probably the Geat king Hrēþel of 374 in another form, which would make the mail a gift of Beowulf's grandfather. ‘Wēlandes geweorc’ is ‘Weland's work’: Weland is the smith of Germanic legend, whose name makes any weapon he is said to have made a famous one.

sentences.t: Gǣð ā wyrd swā hīo scel!’
sentences.l: Goes ever fate as she shall!’
sentences.i: Fate always goes as it is bound to!’
sentences.n: ‘Gǣð’ is the present of ‘gān’, ‘go’; ‘ā’ is ‘ever’; ‘wyrd’ is ‘fate, what comes to be’. ‘swā hīo scel’ is ‘as she shall’: ‘hīo’ is ‘she’, so ‘wyrd’ is feminine, and ‘scel’ is a short spelling of ‘sceal’. The closing mark ends Beowulf's speech and the part.
